patient.chief_complaint: Wife called 911 - husband having continuous left-sided focal seizure spreading to bilateral convulsions, 15 minutes
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Clarke is a 52-year-old man with left temporal focal epilepsy on carbamazepine who is brought by ambulance after his wife called 911 when he developed a focal seizure with left-sided onset involving right hand automatisms and lip smacking, which secondarily generalized after 2 minutes. The seizure has been continuous for 15 minutes. He took his medications yesterday but his wife is not sure about his compliance over the past week as he has been working very long hours with minimal sleep. He started a new 10-day antibiotic course 4 days ago for community-acquired pneumonia — he was prescribed clarithromycin by his primary care physician. He has a documented valproate allergy (thrombocytopenia and pancreatitis). His hypothyroidism is stable on levothyroxine.

results.finding: Clarithromycin is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor - increases carbamazepine levels by 50-100%
Alternative macrolide azithromycin: minimal CYP3A4 inhibition - safer with carbamazepine
Respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin): no significant CYP3A4 interaction
Doxycycline: no significant CYP3A4 interaction with carbamazepine
Complete the CAP treatment course with safe antibiotic to prevent pneumonia relapse

output.summary: Clarithromycin is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor and increases carbamazepine exposure by 50–100%. Alternative agents for community-acquired pneumonia with less CYP3A4 interaction include azithromycin (minimal inhibition), levofloxacin, and doxycycline. Completing the antibiotic course with a non-interacting agent prevents pneumonia relapse.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
DaTscan / dopamine transporter imaging has no role in SE; no parkinsonism question relevant to acute management.

sequence_constraints.reason: ECG must be reviewed for CBZ-induced AV block before further AED loading.

critical_actions: Hold carbamazepine and switch antibiotic (clarithromycin → azithromycin/doxycycline)
Load IV levetiracetam as bridging AED
Continuous cardiac monitoring during CBZ clearance (risk of arrhythmia)
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT continue clarithromycin with carbamazepine — the interaction is the cause
Do NOT load phenytoin in patient with CBZ-induced cardiac effects without monitoring
Do NOT use other CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., erythromycin, fluconazole) with carbamazepine
Do NOT continue clarithromycin with carbamazepine — the interaction is the cause; switch to azithromycin or doxycycline.
key_reasoning_points: Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor; combination with carbamazepine (CYP3A4 substrate) raises CBZ levels into toxic range
CBZ toxicity can cause cardiac AV block / arrhythmia
Switching macrolide to azithromycin (minimal CYP interaction) or doxycycline resolves the interaction
ESETT supports LEV / VPA / fosphenytoin equivalence as second-line

SSRIs at therapeutic doses have minimal seizure threshold effect; CBZ toxicity is the cause
